newsitem.title: USA: Euro seen diluted, not delayed by French vote-poll.
newsitem.headline: Euro seen diluted, not delayed by French vote-poll.

text.p: The sharp leftward turn of French voters on Sunday will probably not delay the debut of the euro, according to a survey of analysts by Reuters.

But a majority of U.S. forecasters expected a watered-down version of the proposed single currency at the planned January 1, 1999 launch date if the new French government holds out for broader membership.

"Once you diminish the criteria, it is very difficult to keep the weaker members out and it's pretty clear the Socialists in France are going to want to weaken the criteria," said Kevin Harris, international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch.
In the second round of voting on Sunday, the French left won 318 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, meaning French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin would take over as Prime Minister on Tuesday.
The Socialists favor a loosening of the conditions for entry outlined in the Maastricht Treaty.
Thirteen currency analysts, out of 15 polled, forecast that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would start on time.

But 13 of 15 experts surveyed also expect the tough criteria for participation -- particularly the requirement that all candidates bring their budget deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product -- to be loosened.
Most (11) also expect a greater number of founding members in the wake of the French election, with Spain, Italy and Portugal likely to be included at kick off time.
Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, said he did not expect a larger group in the first wave of EMU, adding he had always projected Italy to be in the vanguard.
Others, however, expected Spain and Portugal to participate, but not Italy.
"Italy, I think, is a mess," said Craig Larimer, head of international market analysis at First Chicago NBD Bank. "They're in recession and won't cut interest rates."
Of the 15 analysts, five said the political events in France would lead them to revise their forecasts for dollar/mark upward.

"You have to see how this whole thing shakes out and certainly there are people who think (U.S. Treasury bonds) can be a safe haven. You're going to have flows of funds out of European bond markets," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal in Chicago.
"There is no question, in the short run, this is dollar positive," said Johnson, who added that his six-month dollar forecast is unrevised at this point.
The dollar is projected to be stronger, at a rate of 1.7323 marks in six months, based on the average of 13 forecasts provided.
Survey questions:
1) Do you think EMU will go through as planned in January 1999 in light of the French elections?
2) Do you believe the strength of the euro will be undermined by a loosening of the Maastricht criteria?
3) Do you expect a greater number of founding members in the wake of the recent French elections?
4) Does this change your outlook for dollar/mark?
5) What is your six month dollar/mark forecast?
